name: Tomas Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I grow wheat, barley and oilseed rape on three hundred and sixty hectares of flat, heavy ground that my father farmed for thirty-five years. Right now the drilling is done, so my days are checking the crops for slugs, spraying when the wind allows, and selling grain from the store. Most mornings start at the kitchen table at six with coffee and my laptop, looking at the yield maps and grain prices, then I'm out in the pickup by seven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been running it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years, since Dad died. Before that I was an electrician for twenty years, wiring houses and factories. My brother didn't want the farm, so I used my savings and a loan to buy his half, and here I am, forty-three and still asking the agronomist, the crop adviser, what half his words mean.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the technology, honestly. The tractor steers itself by GPS, the sprayer shuts off nozzles so it doesn't double-spray, and I ask an AI every day about prices and disease. What's hard is that Dad knew every wet corner of every field without a map, and I'm learning them one stuck tractor at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first of five pictures of the next five years. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great tool and every farmer should be using it. I'd tell the lads at church who still do everything on paper that it saves me hours. I'd probably post about it, too, I'm on the farmers' forums all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed if that's all it becomes. I think it can do more, and I want my farm on the front edge. But I'd also be fine, because I'm on the land and nobody's replacing the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the better version of the grain-selling tool, about six hundred a year, and use it to time my sales. I'd put a weather station in the far field, around two thousand, because the forecast for town is useless out there. And I'd take my cousin's boy Diego on as an apprentice, because he's eighteen and itching to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit impatient. I want to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Diego.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's my cousin Rosa's son, left school last summer and has been washing cars. He came out at harvest and drove the grain trailer like he was born in it. I'd pay him properly, put him through the college course one day a week, and teach him what Dad taught me, which some days isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think about money right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're in good shape. We've got savings to cover more than a year, and the land behind us, and my wife Isabel has her job as bursar at the secondary school. The loan for my brother's half is the big number, but the land is worth far more than the loan.

S0.say: I'd say it's a great tool every farmer should use, and I'd tell the church lads who do everything on paper that it saves me hours. I'd post about it on the farmers' forums.
S0.think: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed if that's all it becomes, because I want my farm on the front edge. But I'd be fine, because I'm on the land and nobody's replacing the land.
S0.do: Upgrades his grain-selling AI tool for about six hundred a year and installs a two-thousand weather station in the far field. Takes on his eighteen-year-old cousin's son Diego as a paid apprentice with a day a week at college.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit impatient to get on with it.
S0.quote: I'd pay him properly, put him through the college course one day a week, and teach him what Dad taught me, which some days isn't much.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is eager, fast-talking and proud of his gadgets, yet he keeps coming back to his late father's knowledge of the fields. Taking on Diego reflects his belief in apprenticeships and family. His money is secure, and he thinks of the land as the base under everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is how it should be, so businesses can adapt without the government interfering. If firms hire fewer beginners, they're making a mistake, but it's their call. Apprenticeships are the answer, not schemes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, slow suits me fine, because I move faster than most farmers round here. I'd have three or four years of an edge. But I'm a beginner myself, and if the agronomist's firm stops training young advisers, who do I ring in ten years?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the tools that are proven: a drone to scout the crops for disease, about eight thousand, and the AI agronomy service that reads the drone pictures. I'd sell more grain forward, which means agreeing a price months ahead, using the AI to watch the market. And I'd keep Diego on and push him to learn the drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite hopeful, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms hiring fewer beginners is their call. But you're worried about who you'll ring. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, you've got me. I still don't want the government forcing firms to hire, but I'd say it loudly at the farmers' meeting, that we need young agronomists. Pressure from customers, not laws.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mateo, your son, about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo is fifteen and good with computers, so I'd tell him learn a trade first, like I did, then use computers on top. An electrician's ticket never let me down. Lucia, my daughter, wants to be a teacher like her grandmother, and I'd say go for it.

S1.say: I'd say slow is how it should be, so businesses can adapt without government interfering. Firms hiring fewer beginners are making a mistake, but apprenticeships are the answer, not schemes.
S1.think: Privately slow suits me, because I move faster than most farmers around here and I'd have years of an edge. But I'm a beginner too, and if advice firms stop training young agronomists, I wonder who I'll ring in ten years.
S1.do: Buys an eight-thousand crop-scouting drone with an AI service to read the images and sells more grain forward with AI watching the market. Keeps Diego on and has him learn the drone.
S1.fieldNote: When I raised the tension between leaving hiring to firms and his own need for young advisers, he accepted the point and chose pressure over regulation. His enthusiasm for tools is matched by a strong belief in learning a trade first. He thinks about his children's futures in practical, grounded terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get out ahead of it and retrain, and companies should help their own staff do that. I'm wary of politicians promising to fix everything, they usually make it worse. I'd say learn a trade, there's always a shortage of electricians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my first thought is Isabel. She runs the school office, budgets, payroll, orders, and that's exactly what this card describes. If her job goes, we lose a good salary and her pension, and she loves that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Isabel the first weekend and look at what she could do next, maybe take over the farm business side properly, which I'm bad at. I'd use AI agents for the farm paperwork too, because if they can do it for a school they can do it for me. And I'd tell the lads at church who work in offices to come and talk to me about electrical apprenticeships, I still know people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because of Isabel. Otherwise I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Isabel say if you suggested she work on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd laugh first, because she knows I'm hopeless at forms. Then she'd say she doesn't want to be her husband's secretary. Fair enough, so I'd say partner, not secretary, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're happy to use AI agents for your paperwork, the same thing that might take Isabel's job. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortably, if I'm honest. But I can't stop the tide by not using it on my own farm. I'd rather use it and look after my own family than refuse it and change nothing.

S2.say: I'd say people need to get ahead of it and retrain, with companies helping their own staff. I'm wary of politicians promising to fix everything, and there's always a shortage of electricians.
S2.think: Privately my first thought is my wife Isabel, who runs the school office, budgets and payroll, exactly what this card describes. We'd lose a good salary and pension, and she loves that job.
S2.do: Sits down with Isabel the first weekend to plan her next step, possibly as a full partner running the farm business. Uses AI agents for the farm paperwork and points office workers from church toward electrical apprenticeships through his old contacts.
S2.feel: Uneasy because of Isabel; otherwise fine.
S2.quote: Then she'd say she doesn't want to be her husband's secretary. Fair enough, so I'd say partner, not secretary, and I'd mean it.
S2.fieldNote: His enthusiasm for AI collides with his wife's office job, and he admitted the discomfort without backing away from using it. His instinct is to solve through family and his old trade network, not through government. The 'partner, not secretary' line came quickly and with warmth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built and invested in these things deserve the rewards, that's how markets work. But I'd also say the rich have a duty to their towns and churches, and they should give generously without being forced. I'd be suspicious of big new taxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd do well. Land values go up, grain still sells, and I'm in physical work. But my congregation is full of office people, accountants, a solicitor, our pastor's wife in insurance, and I'd be watching my friends go under while my farm grows in value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the forty hectares my neighbour has been offering, using some savings and the boom in land value as security, because good land next door comes up once in a lifetime. I'd set aside money for the church hardship fund, maybe five thousand. And I'd offer harvest work to anyone from church who needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good for us, hard for people I care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying land in a boom, isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I know it. But the land doesn't disappear, it grows wheat whatever the price. I'd borrow carefully, no more than I could cover if prices fell by a third.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd prefer people to give voluntarily rather than be taxed. Would that be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, probably not, if it's as big as this card says. I'd still rather it came through churches and families. But I'd accept some tax on the very biggest gains if it stopped the country tearing itself apart.

S3.say: I'd say those who built and invested in these things deserve the rewards, because that's how markets work. But the rich have a duty to their towns and churches and should give generously without being forced.
S3.think: Privately I think we'd do well, with land values up and grain still selling. But my congregation is full of office people, and I'd be watching friends go under while my farm grows in value.
S3.do: Buys the forty hectares next door, borrowing only what he could cover if prices fell by a third. Gives about five thousand to the church hardship fund and offers harvest work to anyone from church who needs it.
S3.feel: Uneasy: good for his family, hard for people he cares about.
S3.quote: I'd be watching my friends go under while my farm grows in value.
S3.fieldNote: Tomas is honest that this scenario helps him and hurts his community. When pressed, he moved from voluntary giving to accepting some tax on the biggest gains, a real shift. His risk-taking shows in buying land at a high price, but with a clear limit on borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms are the future, and I'd be one of the first to have one. Grain farming already runs on machines, so a tractor that drives itself all night is the obvious next step. I'd say the government should stay out of the way and let farmers choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm excited for the farm and worried for the people. A robot tractor means I don't need Diego at drilling time, and I promised his mum I'd teach him a trade. And if robots go into building sites, my old trade as an electrician isn't the safe bet I told Mateo it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy or lease a self-driving tractor for the first autumn, probably around a hundred and fifty thousand, or lease it to start. I'd put Diego in charge of watching it, fixing it and planning its routes, so he learns the robot rather than losing to it. And I'd change what I tell Mateo: learn to fix the robots, not just wire the houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy at the same time. I'm happy for me and a bit guilty about Diego.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Diego's mother, Rosa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, that the tractor drives itself now, but Diego's the one who keeps it running. I'd show her his pay slip, so she knows he's not just a passenger. And I'd promise again that he's family and he stays, robot or no robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should stay out of it. What about the farmworkers who lose their jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's hard for me. I'd want farms and churches to look after their own first. But if whole villages lose their work, I suppose somebody has to help them retrain, and I'd rather that was apprenticeships than benefits.

S4.say: I'd say robots on farms are the future and I'd be one of the first to have one, because grain farming already runs on machines. The government should stay out of the way and let farmers choose.
S4.think: Privately I'm excited for the farm and worried for the people. A robot tractor means I don't need Diego at drilling time, and robots on building sites mean my old trade isn't the safe bet I told my son it was.
S4.do: Leases a self-driving tractor for the first autumn, worth around a hundred and fifty thousand. Puts Diego in charge of running and fixing it, and tells his son Mateo to learn to fix robots rather than only wire houses.
S4.feel: Excited and uneasy at once: glad for the farm, guilty about Diego.
S4.quote: And if robots go into building sites, my old trade as an electrician isn't the safe bet I told Mateo it was.
S4.fieldNote: He is the only farmer in this group who sees the robot scenario as mainly good for his own business. His guilt is focused on Diego and on the advice he gave his son. On help for displaced workers he keeps reaching for apprenticeships and churches, and admits it may not be enough.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the third, because of Isabel and my friends at church, not because of the farm. The robots I'd welcome on my land. What would help is real apprenticeships, paid properly, for adults, not just school leavers, so a forty-five-year-old accountant can become an electrician or a robot technician without starting at the bottom.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask me what my father would think. He'd hate the robot tractor, I know that. But he'd love that Diego is learning on this land, and that's the part I'd fight to keep.

headlineQuote: He'd hate the robot tractor, I know that. But he'd love that Diego is learning on this land, and that's the part I'd fight to keep.
portrait: Tomas Garcia was an electrician for twenty years before taking over his late father's grain and oilseed farm, buying out his brother with savings and a loan. He is an eager early adopter who uses AI every day, wants his farm on the front edge, and would lease a self-driving tractor the first autumn it was offered. His traditional, free-market views favour apprenticeships, family and church giving over taxes and government schemes, though he softens when pressed on the biggest gains. His worry sits with others: his wife's school office job, friends at church, and the young cousin he promised to train.
biggestWorry: The fast scenario, because it threatens his wife's office job and his friends at church, while the robots he'd welcome on his own farm.
whatWouldHelp: Properly paid apprenticeships for adults, not just school leavers, so people like a mid-career accountant can retrain as electricians or robot technicians.
